title: Apple announces all-new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR display, its first touchscreen Mac
snippet: Apple has officially announced the all-new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR display, its first touchscreen laptop. The new machine was first hinted at by Apple on October 19 with the company’s “Pro and tell” experience teaser. Earlier today, new Apple CEO John Ternus shared a “spotlight” teaser for the laptop as well. Read on for all the details about the new high-end laptop… more…
fullText:
Apple has officially announced the all-new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR display, its first touchscreen laptop.

The new machine was first hinted at by Apple on October 19 with the company’s “Pro and tell” experience teaser. Earlier today, new Apple CEO John Ternus shared a “spotlight” teaser for the laptop as well.

Read on for all the details about the new high-end laptop…  

MacBook Pro details

The new machine features a light-up Apple logo, tandem OLED, and touch input on the display.

It runs on the M5 Pro and M5 Max chips, like the existing MacBook Pro models without OLED touch displays.

John Ternus, who is rocking a new profile picture with the new Mac, shared the first look at the new machine on X:

Apple previously used a glowing Apple logo on its notebook hardware for years until the 12-inch MacBook and 2016 MacBook Pro. 

Pricing for the new laptop starts at $2899 for the 14-inch model. The 16-inch version starts at $3399.

Pre-orders are available starting today with deliveries starting November 6. You can find the product page for the new MacBook Pro here. The new machines are also available on Amazon.

Colors include silver or space black options with standard or nano-texture display configurations.

Beyond the new high-end laptop, Apple also announced the redesigned iPad mini, M6 iMac, and M6 14-inch MacBook Pro this week. Back in March, Apple upgraded the standard 14- and 16-inch MacBook Pro laptops to the current M5 Pro and M5 Max chips.

Apple calls the new design both thinner and lighter than the standard MacBook Pro models in the same size configuration. 

First Mac with touch input

The new MacBook Pro is the first to use what Apple calls a PROLED XDR display, replacing Mini-LED as the MacBook Pro display technology.

While Apple has innovated with multi-touch on the iPhone and iPad, the Mac has been resistant to touch input for years. The new MacBook Pro changes that with the first touchscreen Mac display. Here’s what Apple says about touch on the Mac.

MacBook Pro features Touch for the first time, bringing pros a whole new way to interact with their content. Crafted specifically for the Mac, every touch interaction feels incredibly responsive and refined. Everyday tasks are simple and intuitive, allowing users to scroll through a webpage with a natural swipe; pinch to zoom in on a photo; drag and drop slides from one presentation to another; and double-tap a window to fill the screen, or flick to tile it into place. And the touch sensor is built directly into the display panel — not layered on top of it — reducing latency so users feel like they’re touching the content itself.

Apple also touts the use of a new hinge technology in the MacBook Pro, in part to support touch input without compromising on stability:

Touch also introduces entirely new ways of working for pro users. Graphic designers can now use the entire display as their canvas, no longer constrained by the area of the trackpad when drawing; musicians can play software instruments right onscreen; and app developers can test how Touch performs in their iOS and iPadOS apps directly on the MacBook Pro display. And these new ways to interact with MacBook Pro work in tandem with the keyboard shortcuts and trackpad gestures pros know and love. In addition, a newly designed hinge provides greater stability while using Touch, and advanced video stabilization automatically smooths the camera feed in real time while using Touch on a video call.

In addition to touch as an additional input method, the new MacBook Pro also adopts the Dynamic Island in favor of the notch.

The Dynamic Island now comes to Mac, serving as the home for Spotlight, Live Activities, and Siri AI.

Not interested in touch? The existing MacBook Pro configurations from March stick around at the same prices. You just lose OLED, the glowing Apple logo, and the thinner and lighter design. Performance, however, is pretty much on par between versions as both offer M5 Pro and M5 Max chips.

The new laptops can be configured with up to 128GB of unified memory and 16TB of solid state drive storage.

Peak display brightness jumps from 1600 nits to 2000 nits for HDR content.

	

The 14-inch model is half a pound lighter at just 3 pounds even compared to 3.5 pounds for the same version of the previous design. The overall footprint is reduced as well with 0.59 x 12.24 x 8.52 inch dimensions compared to 0.61 x 12.31 x 8.71 inch dimensions when comparing 14-inch models.

The 16-inch model is notably lighter as well. The new design weighs in at 4 pounds even compared to 4.7 pounds for the previous design. Dimensions change to 0.63 x 14 x 9.62 inches compared to 0.66 x 14.01 x 9.77 inches between designs.

The new machines still use Touch ID with no Face ID support. Apple also doesn’t offer built-in cellular models of the new MacBook Pro. We’ll have to keep waiting for Face ID and built-in cellular connectivity.

You can find Apple’s press release for the new machines here. All configurations are available to order from Amazon.

title: Samsung’s Android XR ‘Intelligent Eyewear’ reportedly launches in December
snippet: Samsung smart glasses in Gentle Monster and Warby Parker styles may finally launch in South Korea and the US before Christmas. more…
fullText:
Samsung smart glasses in Gentle Monster and Warby Parker styles may finally launch in South Korea and the US before Christmas.

It’s been a very long time coming, but one report from ChoSun Biz says that Samsung and Google are finally launching the Samsung Intelligent Eyewear line in the United States and South Korea in mid-December. Curiously, while the report helps set a fuzzy date, there’s still no official price for Samsung’s smart glasses.

Back in July, Samsung teased the price, noting that the company’s first smart glasses will come in at “a reasonable price” for a product “in the premium range.” Presumably, that means Samsung Intelligent Eyewear won’t be shipping at $299 like Meta’s latest smart glasses. Meta’s most premium offering, Oakley Meta Vanguard, retails for $499.

All of the upcoming Samsung Intelligent Eyewear models feature cameras on the front, although it’s possible Samsung will release camera-free glasses sometime in the future.

On Security Bite, it’s one of my favorite pastimes to explain why camera covers are virtually useless today. I’ve been called out plenty of times for it. So when Apple patches a bug that lets a malicious app get access to the camera without permission, I find myself in a rather precarious situation.

This week, Apple released iOS 27.2 to the public, and with it, over 160 different vulnerability patches. One of them fixes a bug that could let a malicious app access an iPhone’s or Mac’s camera without the user’s permission. Rest assured, this is not a hardware issue. Apple’s post-2008 change that put the camera module and the green LED indicator on the same circuit is not at fault here.

The bug, tracked as CVE-2026-86990 and credited to researcher Mustafa Calap, lives in CoreMedia, the framework apps use for audio and video. Apple’s notes only say “an access issue was addressed with improved access restrictions.”

That means the permission prompt, the one that asks whether an app can use your camera, could effectively be skipped entirely. On the Mac, that prompt comes from a system called TCC (Transparency, Consent, and Control), the gatekeeper that’s supposed to keep apps away from your camera until you say yes.

So, am I ordering a camera cover now? No. The green light would still come on (for iPhones that’s the green dot in the status bar rather than a physical LED), because the bug went after the permission, not the indicator. The problem is that the indicator only helps if someone’s there to see it. If you happened to be away from your desk, or your iPhone was face down on the table, there’d be nothing standing between that app and a live feed of the surrounding area.

It’s the exact scenario where tools like Patrick Wardle’s OverSight can come in handy. It’s free, open source application, that alerts you every time the camera or mic turns on and which app triggered it. I use it to log activity on all my Macs. Plastic over the camera can’t do that, huh?

There’s no indication from Apple that this one was exploited in the wild, which is good news here. Still, it’s important to update to iOS 27.2 and macOS Golden Gate 27.2, or iOS 26.7.2 and macOS Tahoe 26.7.2 if you’re holding off on the new OS. Older iPhones like the XS and XR get it in iOS 18.7.11.

And if you’ve never looked, now’s a good time to open Settings > Privacy & Security > Camera on iPhone (System Settings > Privacy & Security > Camera on Mac) and see which apps you’ve actually given access to. You might be surprised to find some that no longer use or don’t recognize.

title: New report on ‘HomeView Ultra’ product covers features, pricing, more
snippet: Apple’s new HomeView product arrives in users’ homes next week, but today a report from The Information outlines what to expect from a larger, high-end ‘HomeView Ultra’ product coming next year. more…
fullText:
Apple’s new HomeView product arrives in users’ homes next week, but today a report from The Information outlines what to expect from a larger, high-end ‘HomeView Ultra’ product coming next year.

Here’s what to expect from larger HomeView-type product with robotic arm

Today Aaron Tilley at The Information published a report on a forthcoming HomeView product that could be dubbed ‘HomeView Ultra.’

Similar to Mark Gurman’s extensive reporting, Tilley classifies the new home product as a robotics project. He says, “Apple’s new CEO John Ternus wants the company to get serious about robots.”

Per the report, the HomeView Ultra product has “a nine-inch screen that swivels around on an arm and resembles the Pixar lamp.” Tilley writes:

Apple initially began working on the robot in 2019—code-naming it J595—and had modest ambitions for it, envisioning it mostly as a device for video calls. Its robotic arm was intended to allow it to follow someone wherever they were in a room. But hopes for the robot ballooned once Apple executives began wanting to add AI capabilities to it.

The current design for the robot envisions it using a camera and sensors to be fully aware of its environment and act autonomously, allowing it to turn on the lights when someone walks into a room—or perhaps even try to tell a cat to get oﬀ a table. It is meant to be smart enough to avoid accidentally hitting objects around it.

The report notes that much of the hardware for the product “has been finished for around two years.” Software, however, is keeping the device from shipping. This is due to a more ambitious slate of AI-powered features than was originally envisioned.

Pricing is expected to be “around $1,000” per the report, but it may cost more depending on market prices for components. Tilley spoke to several former employees who said they expect Apple to use ‘HomeView Ultra’ branding for the product. As we’ve seen this fall though, Apple has been hesitant to expand its slate of Ultra products.

As for release timing, Tilley says that “Apple hopes to launch the robot next year. It could push the launch out to 2028 though.”

title: HomeView could double as a HomeKit security camera, shows code
snippet: Apple code sleuther pdfu has discovered evidence that HomeView will be able to serve as a HomeKit security camera. They found multiple options for the security camera feature, with Apple taking significant steps to protect the privacy of household members … more…
fullText:
Apple code sleuther pdfu has discovered evidence that HomeView will be able to serve as a HomeKit security camera.

They found multiple options for the security camera feature, with Apple taking significant steps to protect the privacy of household members … 

Streaming and recording video from HomeView

Settings discovered in HomeView software 27.2 show settings to use the built-in camera for both streaming and recording.

Off

Your HomeView will not detect motion, stream, or record. Home members will not be able to stream in real-time.

Detect Activity

HomeView will detect motion, but will not stream or record. Home members will not be able to stream in real-time.

Stream

Home members will be able to stream in real-time, but your HomeView will not record.

Stream & Allow Recording

Your HomeView will stream and record. Home members will be able to stream in real-time and view recordings.

Either streaming or recording can be set to activate when you’re home, when you’re away, or when you’re asleep.

Strong privacy protections

As we’d expect from Apple, there are very strong privacy protections for the feature. An indicator light appears on the display when the security camera feature is in use, along with a sound to indicate that streaming or recording has begun. Members of the home also receive a notification.

Additionally, if any home members are in the home, then the security camera feature cannot be remotely activated, only from HomeView itself. This seems likely intended to prevent domestic abusers from spying on their partner.

9to5Mac’s Take

This seems a worthwhile addition to the functionality, and could potentially influence the perceived value of HomeView for anyone on the fence about buying one. The privacy protections are first rate.

title: Elon Musk throttles Grok Bot limits due to ‘unsustainably high’ costs
snippet: Musk recently referred to Grok Bot as having "the fastest growth of a product that I've ever seen in my life."
fullText:
Over Halloween weekend, some Grok Bot users awoke to something especially spooky: their weekly usage limits were unexpectedly maxed out, even if they hadn’t been using SpaceX’s agentic AI overnight. Some users reported on X that their usage jumped from as low as 50% to 100%.

SpaceX CEO Elon Musk confirmed in an X post on Sunday that this was not a glitch.

“The cost of serving Grok Bot was unsustainably high relative to revenue,” he wrote in a reply to a question from a user. He has not addressed the issue on his main feed, but has continued boasting that Grok Bot can help you buy gifts for your family.

The cost of serving Grok Bot was unsustainably high relative to revenue

— Elon Musk (@elonmusk) November 1, 2026

Grok Bot has been positioned as a success story for the newly public SpaceX, which said in a filing last month that AI now makes up 52% of company income. Its renamed “Super Intelligence” division actually turned a profit of $431 million, which is a rarity in the AI industry. Its profit would’ve been higher if not for $1.2 billion of one-time costs related to its acquisition of Cursor. Musk recently referred to Grok Bot as having “the fastest growth of a product that I’ve ever seen in my life.”

Musk has not yet shared how subscribers’ usage limits will be impacted moving forward.

title: Apple memory supplier expects price increases through at least 2030
snippet: Key Apple memory supplier SK Hynix has warned that RAM and flash memory shortages are likely to last through at least 2030, keeping product prices high. Apple is believed to be one of 14 customers who have locked in priority orders, but the contract does not protect against price increases related to the balance of supply and demand … more…
fullText:
Key Apple memory supplier SK Hynix has warned that RAM and flash memory shortages are likely to last through at least 2030, keeping product prices high.

Apple is believed to be one of 14 customers who have locked in priority orders, but the contract does not protect against price increases related to the balance of supply and demand …

The company says that while AI continues to drive demand and growth, there is little that can be done in the short to medium term to increase supply.

Supply, on the other hand, is not keeping pace with the growth of the market. Given technical difficulty of leading-edge processes and the long lead time required to build new production facilities, it expects the structure in which demand exceeds supply to persist through 2030.

The Register reports that SK Hynix has long-term deals with 14 tech giants for priority orders, but these allow for market-based price increases.

14 big buyers […] will collectively buy more than half of its output during 2027 and 2028, and some of them want to extend those agreements. The Korean giant doesn’t mind that because the deals include “a mechanism that reflects market conditions within a price range agreed upon with customers”

Apple is used to being in the driving seat when it comes to negotiating with suppliers, but this is not the case where memory and flash storage is concerned. Here, the shortages mean that it will have been forced to agree to contracts that allow significant price hikes in order to obtain guaranteed supplies.

Nikkei Asia also reports that printed circuit boards may be the next component to experience constrained supply. Once a humble commodity item, advances in the technology has turned them into specialist tech, with more layers and higher bandwidth requirements. The report says “that complexity shrinks the supplier pool and extends lead times.”

Apple said back in June that the company was doing its best to mitigate the price increases, but it has so far been unable to do so.

Apple hardware costs more than it did a year ago, and if you have purchased a fleet recently, you are feeling it. Now, one thing I should mention: Macs have not risen in price with inflation or performance. If you think about what a Mac mini or MacBook Air cost when they launched vs. today, I would still say they are extremely affordable. With that being said, there’s a scenario taking shape in the enterprise where the price of a Mac matters a lot less than it used to. If open-weight AI models become a real part of how companies work, Apple Silicon might end up looking basically free compared to the token bill it supplements.

About Apple @ Work: Bradley Chambers has been an Apple IT admin since 2009. Through his experience deploying and managing firewalls, switches, a mobile device management system, enterprise grade WiFi, 1000s of Macs, and 1000s of iPads, Bradley will highlight ways in which Apple IT managers deploy Apple devices, build networks to support them, train users, share stories from the trenches of IT management, and ways Apple could improve its products for IT departments.

Cloud AI in the enterprise is priced by the token, and that’s a fine model when usage is moderate. The problem is that usage isn’t staying light. Agentic tools that write code, analyze documents, and run multistep tasks consume tokens at a pace a chatbot never did, and the bill scales right along with them. Earlier this year, Fleet’s IT leadership research cited a company that burned through its entire 2026 AI budget in four months after rolling an AI coding tool out to roughly 5,000 engineers. That’s the risk with a variable cost by token usage. Finance is somewhat in the dark on what the number is until the invoice shows up.

Local hardware works the opposite way, where you pay once, and the cost is capped. Every hour that machine spends running a model after that costs you very little, aside from power usage.

ROI on Apple Silicon

Someone I’ve long respected, Horace Dediu, showed some interesting numbers in a recent Asymco piece that really shows the opportunity ahead for Apple. In one example, a 26-billion-parameter model used for analysis four hours a day, around 150 million tokens a month, runs $450 to $850 per user per month through a cloud provider. A 16″ MacBook Pro with an M5 Max and 128GB of unified memory costs about $6,500 and can run a model locally. That’s a payback period of 7 to 14 months. He gives a lot more examples, and it’s worth a read to see Apple’s opportunity here.

The reason Apple Silicon is so well suited to this is unified memory. On most PCs, the GPU has its own small memory pool, and the model has to fit within it. On Apple Silicon, the GPU shares the entire memory pool, so a laptop with 128GB can hold a model that would need a far more expensive setup elsewhere.

Viewed through this lens, a price increase on a Mac Studio is a rounding error. If the machine pays for itself in under a year, and Apple Silicon Macs can stay in service for four to five years, it’s practically free over a normal refresh cycle. Now, if agentic coding keeps improving at such a rapid pace, you might end up upgrading sooner than that.

Wrap up: the big if with open-weight models

All of this hinges on one assumption: the math only works if an open-weight model running locally is good enough for your task day-to-day. For a lot of everyday work, like summarizing docs, drafting, content analysis on internal data, and basic routine coding, the gap between open-weight models and the frontier has narrowed significantly recently. For the hardest reasoning and coding tasks, frontier models still lead, and that isn’t changing anytime soon.

There are other caveats, too: his usage figures in those examples are high, and a typical employee isn’t burning through 150 million tokens a month. Token prices have also been falling, narrowing the gap over time. I am really interested in a hybrid model as well. Cribl recently launched StreamAI, an AI gateway for telemetry that routes each prompt to the right model and includes built-in budget control. At JNUC 2026, Jamf showed on-device AI support that deploys models through blueprints, routes prompts through an on-device AI gateway, and governs all of it with AI policies. Apple is clearly thinking about this too. At JNUC, Apple’s Jeremy Butcher had this to say regarding cloud and on-device AI:

“We think our platform makes for the best way to do both,” said Butcher. “We continue to have these conversations, and we look forward to working with all of you to bring it to life.”

A hybrid model might be the best of both worlds, with routine work running locally and the hardest tasks routed to frontier models in the cloud. Either way, Apple is well positioned. Even with RAM and GPU shortages driving up hardware prices, the ROI on Apple Silicon looks promising if open-weight models end up handling a decent share of enterprise AI workloads. Mac prices are going up, but token bills are going up faster (even if token prices continue to fall).

title: Here’s what ‘renoa’ — the first new fiber in 25 years — feels like
snippet: Startup Everbloom's new material, renoa, is the first new fiber in 25 years, and it feels very familiar.
fullText:
Sometimes it seems like everyone — and every occasion — demands cashmere these days.

Numerous brands sell cashmere sweaters, from Bruno Cucinelli’s $7,900 cable knit cardigan to Quince’s $50 crewneck. Menswear company Loro Piana has made cashmere a cornerstone of its lineup, helping to drive the LVMH division’s valuation above €11 billion. There are even cashmere running shirts.

But as cashmere has spread throughout the fashion industry, it’s not for everyone. It’s still relatively expensive, hard to care for, and environmental fraught. The goats that produce cashmere have been trashing rangelands across Central Asia. 

That may change, though. I recently experienced an alternative fiber called renoa, developed by a startup called Everbloom, that’s washable and promises to be more affordable. It could bring the cashmere experience, via a substitute material, to more products and people.

Everbloom has made a number of sample items using renoa, including this glove and scarf. The scarf has been washed and dried in a tumble dryer.Image Credits:Tim De Chant/TechCrunch

Renoa is made from sources of waste protein, including cashmere and wool scraps as well as down and feather “lint” leftover from the bedding industry. Everbloom processes the waste into a powder and blends it with a biodegradable biopolymer, and the combination is then extruded to the right length and diameter to mimic specific natural fibers.

Renoa was recently approved as the first new fiber classification in 25 years by the U.S. Federal Trade Commission, which regulates fiber labeling in the U.S.

Everbloom has been developing the new fiber for three years, and is currently in the process of scaling up. The startup developed its own AI model for material science, and a cashmere substitute is the first product.

Last month, I stopped by Everbloom’s headquarters in New York City, which sits 15 floors above 5th Avenue, kitty corner from Bryant Park. There, co-founder and CEO Sim Gulati walked me through a range of products made with its company’s cashmere-like renoa, including a crewneck sweater, a pair of knit gloves, and a scarf.

The sweater and gloves were soft and light, but the scarf was the most notable. It didn’t look like much, but it had been through the kind of hell and back that a pure cashmere scarf wouldn’t survive. It was a custom item that Everbloom had knit to test renoa, and Gulati had been wearing and washing it for months, including a trip through the tumble dryer before I saw it. It wasn’t pilled, and Gulati said it hadn’t shrunk, either.

Waste feathers (left) are ground into a powder (second from left) and combined with a biopolymer to make pellets ready for an extruder (second from right).Image Credits:Tim De Chant/TechCrunch

Everbloom is currently working with a range of companies to get renoa into consumer products. The first are likely to feature renoa as a blended fiber, making up around 20% of the material in a cashmere sweater, for example. The first product is expected to hit the market in the second quarter of 2027 Gulati said.

The 80/20 cashmere-renoa blend that I felt was extremely close to the real thing, and Gulati said that additional finishing that accompanies commercial garments should eliminate any differences without compromising the washability and stability of the garment. After my visit, I kept thinking about various items in my closet that could benefit from those features. When renoa lands on shelves next year, I’ll be keeping an eye out for it.

title: SpaceX reportedly wants to buy Boost Mobile to compete with AT&T, T-Mobile, and Verizon
snippet: SpaceX has been looking for new ways to use its Starlink network, and a tie-up with cellular operator Boost Mobile could give it the terrestrial access it needs.
fullText:
SpaceX is looking to buy Boost Mobile from EchoStar, according to a report from The Washington Post. If the deal goes through, it would help the Elon Musk-owned company build a hybrid cellular-satellite network that could help catapult it into fourth place among the top U.S. wireless providers.

The space-launch company has been dabbling in cellular connectivity, rolling out satellite access to T-Mobile’s subscribers in 2024. Last year, SpaceX bought $17 billion worth of wireless spectrum from EchoStar for cellular services, which could help the company’s Starlink service reach inside buildings, for example, something it currently struggles with.

“This is the last critical piece of the spectrum puzzle needed for SpaceX to provide complete phone coverage in America,” Musk said on X at the time of the spectrum acquisition. Yet, if Musk is still looking to buy access to terrestrial networks, it apparently wasn’t the last piece.

Elon Musk, SpaceX’s CEO, reportedly spoke directly with EchoStar chairman Charlie Ergen in October about acquiring Boost Mobile, the mobile virtual network operator. EchoStar has about 7.5 million customers between Boost Mobile and GenMobile, its other mobile service offering.

Musk has also approached AT&T, T-Mobile, and Verizon about buying capacity on their networks. All three rejected Musk, and they may still have a say in a SpaceX acquisition of Boost Mobile. Boost doesn’t operate its own towers, instead leasing capacity from AT&T and T-Mobile, which might need to approve such a deal. Sources speaking to The Post said that network leases are usually nontransferable.

The big three providers each have over 100 million subscribers, dwarfing Boost Mobile. But while the acquisition would give SpaceX an immediate bump in subscribers, the true value of the deal would be giving the company access to terrestrial cellular networks. 

Gaining access to towers leased to Boost Mobile would expand coverage significantly — Boost currently covers most of the 48 contiguous states in the U.S. — allowing Starlink to cover devices when they’re outdoors and relying on cell towers to handle devices when Starlink signals can’t reach them.

title: Google stock drops amid AI fears; AI Mode has ‘lower monetization,’ getting more ads
snippet: Google is bringing ads to AI Mode globally as it admits that the new take on Search brings “lower monetization,” all while $GOOG stock is seeing a fairly major drop. more…
fullText:
Google is bringing ads to AI Mode globally as it admits that the new take on Search brings “lower monetization,” all while $GOOG stock is seeing a fairly major drop.

Alphabet’s Q3 earnings call yesterday saw Google’s Philipp Schindler acknowledging that AI Mode, the company’s Gemini-powered new take on Search, has “lower monetization” compared to traditional Search. So the “strong growth” of AI Mode didn’t have as much of a positive impact on  Google’s bottom line simply because the mode doesn’t generate as much revenue.

Schindler said:

…It’s worth noting that the strong growth in AI Mode queries had an impact because of the lower monetization we’re seeing in AI Mode. To be clear, we feel very good about our trajectory here. Our ad experiments have shown promising results and we’re now scaling ads within both AI Overviews and AI Mode to more users and more queries…

In a blog post the same day, Google announced that AI Mode would be getting ads in global markets. US users will also start to see “multiturn ads” in follow-up queries.

	

Our research shows that people are comfortable with ads in AI Mode and find them highly relevant. In fact, click-through rates are already similar between sponsored and organic product list items within AI Mode.

Now we’re scaling ads in AI Mode in Australia, Canada, India, Kenya, Malaysia, New Zealand, Nigeria, Pakistan, the Philippines, and Singapore. In Q4 2026, we plan to expand to additional locales, including Brazil, Mexico, and the United Kingdom.

Meanwhile, $GOOG stock dipped by 27 points around the time of the earnings call and has continued to drop on October 29. It currently sits around $280, just a few points higher than a March 30 low of $273.14. The 12% drop reduces Google’s market cap by over $500 billion. NBC News points out that it is the second-biggest drop behind Nvidia’s $589 billion drop in 2025.

The drop is not directly due to AI Mode itself, but is attributed to weaker-than-expected earnings in Q3. Ad revenue from Search still makes up roughly half of Google’s overall revenue.

Our Daniel Bader expands on this in the latest issue of Inbox, our twice-weekly free newsletter:

Google had a very good, very bad Q3

…But investors are looking at the capital expenditure tied up in future data center buildouts and getting nervous that, if the bubble bursts, even these well-capitalized companies will take massive hits.

The biggest question surrounding Google’s stock performance is whether it can sufficiently monetize AI-powered search before demand for its traditional search inventory falls off a cliff. As the company sends less and less traffic to the open web, it’s touting the fact that AI Mode and AI Overviews keep people on Google for three times as long as traditional search.

title: Public Discord messages might start showing up in Google Search, unless users opt out
snippet: Discord announced today that Discoverable Server web pages will begin showing summaries and pulled content, which might show up in search engines. more…
fullText:
Discord announced today that Discoverable Server web pages will begin showing summaries and pulled content, which might show up in search engines.

Discord splits its servers into three different types: private, community, and discoverable. The latter is the most public version. No one needs an invite, and anyone can message, given that the admins of that server haven’t blocked you completely.

In a recent press release, Discord notes that all Discoverable Servers will get a Server Web Page. The page is essentially an overall summary of that server, so users can easily gauge whether they its something they want to join.

Discord says that discussion summaries will also appear on those server web pages, extracted from public channels. Any conversation that might be deemed noteworthy, whether by an AI model or moderator, could appear on that web page, and by extension, search engines like Google.

	

It sounds like Discord is hoping channels surface in Google’s AI Mode or other engines, like Reddit, when users search for certain topics. It’s not a bad idea, as message boards often contain answers to incredibly niche questions otherwise hard to find on the internet.

The release makes it clear that server admins can exclude certain channels and channel summaries, but doesn’t say the entire server can opt out. That seems to only be possible by switching server types.

Individual users can also opt out. Users can head to User Settings > Data and Privacy to control whether their public messages appear in the server web page.

Discord says these changes will take effect starting November 16. Admins and users wishing to opt out of having their public messages and channels included in web pages, and by extension, search results, will need to opt out before then.

title: Ninja’s first-ever microwave just replaced two of my kitchen appliances at once
snippet: The Ninja Crispi Microwave stands out for its FusionCrisp technology, which combines the speed of a microwave with the crispy results you'd expect from an air fryer.
fullText:
I never thought I’d get excited about replacing my microwave, but the Ninja Crispi Microwave and Air Fryer has made a pretty convincing case for ditching two appliances and making room for one. Combining a microwave with a built-in air fryer, it’s designed to speed up everyday cooking, give leftovers their crunch back and, perhaps best of all, free up some valuable kitchen counter space.

Priced at $449.99, it’s certainly not a budget-friendly microwave. But this is no ordinary machine for heating leftover soup. Ninja has paired a 1,000W microwave with a 1,700W air fryer system, powered by its FusionCrisp technology, which combines the speed of microwave cooking with the golden, crispy results you’d typically expect from an air fryer.

Think leftover pizza, chicken tenders, fries, and all those foods that tend to turn sad and soggy in a traditional microwave. Instead, the idea is to get food that’s piping hot and juicy on the inside, with a deliciously crisp, golden finish on the outside. In other words, no more choosing between speed and texture.

Image Credits:Ninja

Of course, microwave and air fryer combinations aren’t entirely new. Brands such as Smeg have already explored the concept, while plenty of modern microwaves come with a range of additional cooking functions. 

What makes the Ninja Crispi Microwave particularly interesting, however, is its FusionCrisp technology, which is designed to bring both cooking methods together rather than simply offering two separate functions. It comes with a 5.5-quart glass cooking dish and a nonstick crisper plate, which sits on top when you want to air fry and crisp up your food. 

Another part that makes it stand out is that there isn’t a rotating plate inside, opening up a lot more space to cook more dishes at once.

It’s not just about reheating leftovers. For example, if you want to make a pasta bake, the microwave can cook the pasta, while the air fryer crisps up the cheese on top. 

There’s one thing to consider before buying it, though. Measuring 20.3 x 17.56 x 14.1 inches, the microwave is hardly compact. It takes up a fair amount of counter space, so while it could free up room if you’re replacing a separate microwave and air fryer, it’s not necessarily the ideal solution for a small apartment kitchen.

Then there’s the $449.99 price tag. That’s a considerable amount to spend on a microwave, particularly when a basic model can handle everyday reheating for a fraction of the cost. But if you’re someone who regularly reaches for both a microwave and an air fryer, the combination could make a lot more sense.

title: Apple wins expanded access to evidence in OpenAI trade secrets lawsuit
snippet: Apple has scored another win in its trade secrets misappropriation lawsuit against two former employees, OpenAI, and io Products. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Apple has scored another win in its trade secrets misappropriation lawsuit against two former employees, OpenAI, and io Products. Here are the details.

A bit of context

Earlier this month, Judge Edward Davila granted some of Apple’s requests for expedited discovery in the lawsuit where the company accuses two former employees (Chang Liu and Tang Tan), as well as OpenAI and io Products, of trade secret misappropriation.

As we’ve been covering since July, Apple filed this lawsuit accusing the defendants of improperly accessing or using confidential information about its products and technologies to help advance OpenAI’s consumer hardware development efforts.

As part of the lawsuit, Apple asked Judge Davila to issue a preliminary injunction (aimed at preventing the defendants from further using its alleged trade secrets), as well as expedited discovery to obtain early access to internal documents, forensic evidence, and employee testimony.

In his decision partially granting Apple’s request for expedited discovery, Judge Davila gave the company early access to select internal documents, forensic evidence, and employee testimony.

However, he postponed ruling on several other requests, finding Apple’s definition of “Apple Originated Information” too broad.

Following the decision, Apple and the defendants agreed on a narrower definition of the term, which Judge Davila has now adopted (with modifications), allowing Apple to pursue additional discovery.

Today’s decision

In his new decision, Judge Davila granted several of Apple’s previously deferred requests, expanding the company’s access to records concerning its former employees’ handling of confidential information, their use of AI tools, and OpenAI’s recruitment and hardware development practices.

That includes:

Records of Liu’s use of ChatGPT, Claude, Codex, OpenClaw, and other AI tools, including on personal and corporate devices and accounts.

Details about devices, accounts, and messaging apps Liu and Tan allegedly used to access, store, or share confidential Apple information.

Details about any confidential Apple information that may have been deleted or destroyed, including when, how, why, and by whom

Testimony from OpenAI and io Products representatives about work involving Apple information related to batteries, power management, and metal finishing.

Testimony about OpenAI’s interviews involving Apple employees, including whether confidential Apple information was discussed or solicited.

Testimony about steps OpenAI took (or failed to take) to prevent unauthorized use or disclosure of Apple information.

That said, he also denied Apple’s requests for details about OpenAI’s own devices and accounts, its internal investigations, and any potential deletion of confidential Apple information.

He also denied two additional requests for corporate testimony, finding that they were “too broad at this stage and better suited for merits discovery,” meaning Apple can pursue them through the regular discovery process.

Under the new order, the defendants have up to 14 days to produce the requested records and respond to Apple’s questions.

title: Firefox’s AI-powered Smart Window gets form autofill and website monitoring
snippet: Mozilla today announced two new features for Smart Window, its opt-in AI-powered browsing experience in Firefox. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Mozilla today announced two new features for Smart Window, its opt-in AI-powered browsing experience in Firefox. Here are the details.

Smart Window adds two features

Nearly one year ago, Mozilla announced plans to introduce AI Window, an opt-in experience that would let Firefox users interact with an AI assistant while browsing, with features like summarizing content, comparing information across tabs, and answering questions without leaving the browser.

Since then, the feature has been renamed Smart Window, and it has gradually gained new capabilities.

A few months ago, for instance, Mozilla introduced AI-powered web search to Smart Window, alongside automatic tab grouping, duplicate tab detection, and the ability to search browsing history using natural language.

Today, the company announced two additional features rolling out to Smart Window beta users: AI-powered form filling and website monitoring.

As Mozilla explains, the AI-powered form-filling feature can draw context from other open tabs to suggest answers for web forms. This means it goes beyond traditional autofill, which typically handles basic information like names, addresses, and contact details, by generating responses based on information found on other currently open pages.

Here’s Mozilla:

For example, Smart Window could use information from your online portfolio or professional profile to fill in your work history, or draw on those details to draft an answer to a question like “Tell me about a time when…” Firefox’s regular autofill still handles saved information such as your name and address, which can be entered directly into forms without relying on AI models.

Mozilla notes that the feature relies on Google’s Gemini 3.1 Flash Lite model to analyze form fields and extract relevant information from selected tabs, meaning that information from those pages is shared with the AI model for processing.

The second feature rolling out today is website monitoring, which works similarly to Safari’s new “Notify Me” feature introduced with iOS 27 and macOS 27.

It lets users type /watch in the Smart Window chat to tell Firefox to monitor webpages for specific changes, such as price drops, product availability, or new job listings. Firefox then notifies users when those changes are detected.

Users can choose between daily and weekly checks, with up to 5 webpages per task, though monitoring runs only while Firefox is open.

Here’s Mozilla again:

When there’s a match, you’ll see an update through the Tasks button in the toolbar. With desktop notifications enabled, Firefox can also notify you directly; click the notification to open the watched pages. You can have up to 15 active tasks at a time, and you can edit, pause or delete tasks. Smart Window will automatically pause tasks after 60 days without a matching change. If 90 days pass without a change, it will stop checking altogether.

As with AI-powered form filling, the feature relies on an AI model to process information, although in this case Mozilla uses Qwen to identify changes that match what users are looking for.

Both new features are now available in the Smart Window beta for Firefox desktop, though they’re currently limited to English-language users in the US and Canada. Mozilla says they will “roll out to additional markets in the coming months.”

title: Google rolling out software updates for these Nest Cam and Doorbell models
snippet: Alongside updates to several of its other smart home devices, Google is rolling out software updates to several Nest Cam and Doorbell models. more…
fullText:
Alongside updates to several of its other smart home devices, Google is rolling out software updates to several Nest Cam and Doorbell models.

As it continues support, Google is rolling out software updates to six of its older Nest Cam and Doorbell models. The list includes:

Nest Cam Indoor (1st gen)

Nest Cam Outdoor (1st gen)

Nest Hello / Nest Doorbell (wired, 1st gen)

Nest Cam IQ Indoor

Nest Cam IQ Outdoor

Google does note that these updates are only available if you have migrated older Nest devices to the Google Home app, a process that’s been widely available to all users and Nest devices for months, if not years.  

Also noteworthy here is that Google is referring to Nest Hello, its original doorbell camera, as “Nest Doorbell (wired, 1st gen).” 

	

What do these updates actually bring?

Google details a changelog including improvements to Wi-Fi reconnections, faster Night Vision switching, and a fix for the status light on Nest Cam IQ.

Improved Wi-Fi reconnection stability: Fixed issues that could cause cameras to crash or stall when reconnecting after brief Wi-Fi interruptions.

Faster night vision switching when turning on the camera: Fixed an issue on Nest Cam Indoor (1st gen) and Nest Cam Outdoor (1st gen) where turning the camera on in low light or switching to night vision in the Google Home app could take 15 to 20 seconds.

Synchronized audio and video on Nest Doorbell (wired, 1st gen): Fixed an issue that could cause audio and video to fall out of sync and trigger unexpected device restarts.

Accurate status light behavior on Nest Cam IQ: Fixed an issue on Nest Cam IQ Indoor and Nest Cam IQ Outdoor where the status light ring could pulse blue (indicating it was waiting for setup) when Wi-Fi was disconnected on an already set up camera.

These updates are rolling out now and will install automatically in the background.

title: In one of the largest deals in tech history, Marvell buys Lumentum for $115B
snippet: Marvell's planned purchase of Lumentum is one of the biggest acquisitions in tech history. And they both have the same strategic investor: Nvidia.
fullText:
Custom chip designer Marvell has signed a deal to acquire optical chip and networking equipment maker Lumentum in an all-stock deal with an enterprise value of $115 billion (including debt) and an equity value of about $80 billion. Marvell will provide 4.5 shares of its common stock for each share of Lumentum. 

This makes the deal one of the biggest acquisitions in tech history. It compares to Microsoft buying Activision Blizzard for $68.7 billion in 2022 and Dell buying EMC for $67 billion in 2016. 

Interestingly, the two companies have one major shareholder in common: Nvidia. In March, as part of a multi-year agreement to purchase Lumentum’s advanced laser components, the GPU giant invested $2 billion to support Lumentum’s R&D efforts and fab expansion. Later that same month, Marvell announced that Nvidia invested $2 billion in an effort to beef up Marvell’s optical networking and chips portfolio.

With Lumentum, Marvell says it will become a leader in AI connectivity, with products that range from chips to data centers. The transaction is expected to close in the first half of calendar year 2028, should both companies’ shareholders, and regulators, agree.

title: AI apps with hidden sexual and violent deepfake features made it into the App Store
snippet: Hundreds of AI apps with hidden sexual and violent deepfake features made it into Apple’s App Store after passing app review. The same apps were also available in the Google Play Store. An investigation discovered more than 400 apps, apparently created by a single Chinese organization. The apps allow users to upload photos and then generate sexual and violent deepfakes which could be used to humiliate or threaten victims … more…
fullText:
Hundreds of AI apps with hidden sexual and violent deepfake features made it into Apple’s App Store after passing app review. The same apps were also available in the Google Play Store.

An investigation discovered more than 400 apps, apparently created by a single Chinese organization. The apps allow users to upload photos and then generate sexual and violent deepfakes which could be used to humiliate or threaten victims …

A Wired investigation discovered a network of more than 400 connected domains and apps with hidden abusive functionality.

Apps like Viefur [ostentibly used to add clothing to pet photos] often claim to be everyday services—such as language tuition or AI workout coaches. When accessed under certain conditions, however, apps in the network stealthily load a web interface allowing the generation of explicit AI sexual images and videos using photos users upload. The apps include AI scenes such as “bedroom rape” and “threatening knife,” where a man holds a knife to a woman’s neck.

Wired says that the network is “hiding in plain sight,” thanks to thousands of video ads for them published on Facebook and Instagram. Some of the apps have been around for a year and have passed review by Apple, Google, and Meta despite each having clear policies prohibiting harmful deepfake content.

Bait-and-switch tactics were used to pass app review. The apps normally show benign content, but a server check can activate the hidden features. Downloading the app after tapping an ad for the deepfake functionality on Meta platforms appears to be one of the triggers. Dozens of pornography photo and video templates can then be downloaded, with credits purchased to generate deepfakes from user-uploaded photos.

Apple removed 19 apps after Wired shared details.

We review every app before it’s published, and these apps complied with our rules when we reviewed them. After approval, their developers changed the website the app pulls its content from, replacing what we approved with pornographic content, and promoted it through pornographic ads hosted on a third-party platform.

The company recently strengthened protections against this approach. Meta says it has taken action against more than 10,000 ad accounts linked to domains associated with these apps.

title: John Ternus used one word to describe his focus as Apple CEO
snippet: Apple has launched a wave of major new products since John Ternus took over as CEO, and a new interview with Ternus reveals how this aligns very much with his primary focus. more…
fullText:
Apple has launched a wave of major new products since John Ternus took over as CEO, and a new interview with Ternus reveals how this aligns very much with his primary focus.

John Ternus names ‘product’ as the chief thing he’s passionate about and focused on

Following Apple’s unveil of the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR earlier this week, CEO John Ternus sat down for an interview with Steven Levy at WIRED.

Much of the ground covered is familiar territory, with Ternus repeating things he’s said before.

But a standout focus that Ternus emphasizes, echoed by quotes from some of his top executives, is his deep passion for one thing: product. 

Here’s Levy:

I asked Ternus what it’s like to take on a massively expanded portfolio. “One of the amazing privileges of this job is getting to learn so many new things,” he said. “I have been and will continue to learn and go deeper into different areas. But, you know, I do love product. I’m super passionate about it.”

	

This emphasis on product is ever-present in Ternus’s answers to other questions. For example:

On Apple’s AI approach: “I would hope people recognize that the work we do is building incredible products that make their lives better. We’re absolutely going to leverage AI to do that.”

snippet: In an announcement on Monday, OpenAI says it will pilot its "Grid Protectors Program" at an upcoming data center in Effingham County, Georgia, where the company promises to free up to 1,000 megawatts of power during extreme weather or emergencies, enough to power air conditioners in around 700,000 homes. fullText:
In an announcement on Monday, OpenAI says it will pilot its “Grid Protectors Program” at an upcoming data center in Effingham County, Georgia, where the company promises to free up to 1,000 megawatts of power during extreme weather or emergencies, enough to power air conditioners in around 700,000 homes.

The announcement comes as opposition to data centers spreads across the US, in response to massive projects that have begun development and construction, frequently with little or no input from local residents. In Utah, residents protested after Box Elder County commissioners signed off on a data center expected to consume more than double the state’s peak electricity demand in 2025, and spread hot air in the desert valley surrounding the data center.

Now OpenAI’s approach is to pitch the construction of power plants that feed the electricity required by the new AI data centers it’s building as “a resource that utilities can call on when communities need it most.”

Several states like Tennessee, Florida, Oklahoma, Oregon, and others have enacted laws that say they will prevent AI companies from passing energy costs on to residents, in addition to moratoriums and other restrictions. This is besides the environmental impacts, as a recent study by the Houston Advanced Research Center (HARC) said that powering proposed Texas data center projects could undo decades of air quality gains over just five years.

OpenAI, which has switched to calling its AI data centers “compute campuses” in an effort to separate from their poor public reputation, claims it helps reduce costs for customers by operating year-round:

“Electricity demand also rises and falls with the seasons, with different regions facing their biggest peaks at different times,” OpenAI’s announcement says. “Our compute campuses need power year-round. With the right agreements, that steady demand can help spread the grid’s fixed costs across more electricity sales, while flexibility lets us reduce demand when the system is busiest.”

OpenAI says it’s going to continue working with policymakers and utility services to make “arrangements for our future campus to reduce electricity demand when the grid is under strain.” Along with its data center in Georgia, OpenAI is also partnering with Oracle and SoftBank to build its “Stargate” data centers across the US, including in Shackelford County, Texas; Doña Ana County, New Mexico; and Milam County, Texas.

title: Using AI to Vibe Code Your TV Is Stupid
snippet: No one likes clunky TV interfaces or their activity being tracked, but using AI isn’t how to avoid it. There’s an easier way.
fullText:
Recently, some posts on X/Twitter and discussed elsewhere have claimed that AI has helped people “vibe code” their way to a better TV interface. Less clutter, no ads, less tracking and more are all ascribed to AI’s magical powers. Not only is this nonsense, but it’s also stupid. 

First, let me say up front that I understand the frustration. TV interfaces have gotten bloated; they often have ads, and their creepy and invasive tracking properties have long been discussed and warned about by me and others. 

That said, AI is not doing anything unique here. Not only can you do this without AI, but it’s also probably better if you don’t. Using AI risks potentially TV-ruining issues or worse.

			

More from CNET

What’s happening

“Vibe coding” is the colloquial term for using AI to assist or fully write programming code for apps, websites and so on. Instead of learning a programming language, people tell AI agents in plain English (or their language of choice) what they want, and the AI does it, or at least something close to it. 

In this case, people are claiming they’re using an AI agent, usually Claude, to write a new operating system for TVs. This “new” OS is, they claim, faster, easier to use, has no ads and so on.

Why it’s a bad idea 

As with all claims about AI, you should be suspicious. First, TV operating systems are far more complex than they appear. Messing around “under the hood,” especially with no programming knowledge, can easily cause serious problems.

One TV engineer I spoke to for this article, who asked to remain anonymous, literally laughed out loud when I asked him about this. He explained that his engineers will often fix one bug in their software, and it will cause 10 other bugs in random, seemingly unrelated parts of the TV. That’s pretty typical with software development, by the way. There are reports already that people have “bricked” their TVs trying this. As in, they turned their TV into an expensive and unusable brick.

The Google TV interface on a Sony Bravia 9 II.Ty Pendlebury/CNET

There are also a lot of potential issues down the road, even if you have initial success. For instance, will the new vibe-coded OS actually run Netflix and other apps? They might seem to load and then not be able to play anything. What happens if one of the apps needs an update? Will you still be able to? What if that update requires a specific Android version? Maybe you won’t have any issues, but there’s no guarantee of that, and if you don’t have any background in software or coding, can you be sure that more AI vibe coding will fix the issue? Will you be able to perform a factory reset and restore it to the way it was when you bought it? Hopefully yes, but not necessarily.

If you’re not a programmer, how sure are you that the code you’re using is secure? How sure are you that it’s only doing what you want and not exposing your TV to external access? This isn’t as likely as just breaking your TV, but if you don’t know or understand what’s going on “under the hood,” can you really be sure?

And what’s the end goal here? If it’s a faster interface with fewer ads, you can do that already without AI, as I’ll discuss in the next section. If it’s to minimize tracking, maybe changing the OS or interface will help, but not entirely.

Why it’s really stupid: An easier solution already exists

AI can’t invent anything, and you can already change your TV’s interface with just an app install. Android TV launchers, as in the user interface, can be swapped out. So if your TV runs on Android, you can change the interface without any AI vibe coding. These launchers are often far simpler than the stock Google TV interface and are highly customizable. 

Projectivy Launcher

Launchers like Projectivity, Monet and TV Launcher Premium Smart UI are some of the top-rated and most popular ones. The AT4K Launcher even makes your Android TV interface look like the Apple TV interface. There are many more options.

If you have a TV with a company-specific operating system, like LG’s webOS, Samsung’s Tizen, Hisense’s VIDAA and so on, the AI vibe coding trick isn’t likely to work anyway. Companies do their best to lock down their operating systems to prevent exactly the kind of thing we’re talking about here. 

Monet Launcher

It’s entirely arguable that AI wasn’t doing anything clever in the first place. It was just regurgitating what human programmers had already figured out.

What you can do instead

I think there’s a hilarious irony in not wanting your personal data to be out there, so in order to block your TV from tracking you, you give your personal data to AI. If you don’t understand why that’s ironic, you definitely shouldn’t give your data to AI. As I’ve talked about before, there is no easy way to prevent your TV from tracking you and selling your data. You can minimize it, or go to more extreme measures like Pi-holes and not connecting it to the internet at all, but then you’ll just be switching which device is tracking you. Still want streaming? All the streaming devices track you to some extent (the Apple TV 4K less so). 

AT4K Launcher

Using AI to vibe code your way into a better TV experience, however, is a dumb idea. Try a launcher app first and see if that gets you most or all the way to what you’re looking for. Will it be a magical fix to speed up a slow TV? No, but it could be much closer to what you’re looking for, and it’s far less likely to nuke your TV. If you want to go even further, there are apps that give you even more control, but with more potential for issues. Or hey, if you have a TV you don’t mind ruining, and you want to see what you can come up with using an AI that is just stealing from other people’s work, go for it.

title: iPhone Duo could capture nearly 30% of foldable market in 2027, per report
snippet: In a report released today, TrendForce says that with strong demand for the iPhone Duo out of the gate, Apple is poised to capture nearly 30% of the global foldable smartphone market by 2027. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
In a report released today, TrendForce says that with strong demand for the iPhone Duo out of the gate, Apple is poised to capture nearly 30% of the global foldable smartphone market by 2027. Here are the details.

One day after Apple announced the iPhone Duo last month, TrendForce published a report predicting that the company would ship 5 million units of its first foldable iPhone by the end of 2026, capturing 24.8% of the segment.

At the time, TrendForce expected the overall foldable smartphone market to grow by just 0.5% in 2026, with shipments from Android brands alone falling by more than 20% year over year.

By contrast, TrendForce expected the market to reach 23.5 million shipments in 2027, a 16.3% increase. The firm also suggested that Apple’s entry could help drive future growth through improvements in foldable technology, while new AI use cases could further boost demand.

With the iPhone Duo now shipping for nearly a week, TrendForce published a new report today reiterating its previous projections and forecasting that Apple will capture 29.8% of the foldable smartphone market in 2027.

	

From the report:

TrendForce notes that Apple’s greatest advantage lies in its ability to integrate chips, operating systems, and its developer ecosystem. As app compatibility and hardware reliability improve, the Duo is expected to further expand the practical value of foldable displays, helping shift competition in the foldable smartphone market from form-factor innovation toward multitasking efficiency.

If TrendForce’s projections pan out, Apple will hold second place in the foldable smartphone market in 2027, behind Samsung, whose share is expected to fall from 35.1% in 2026 to 31.9% next year, and ahead of Huawei, which is projected to drop from 24.8% to 21.3%.

title: AO3 Suffers Major Outage: Possibly No Fanfic for 2 Weeks or Longer
snippet: Archive of Our Own, one of the world’s biggest fanfiction sites, went down hard as a response to a “security incident.”
fullText:
October has been a rocky month for readers of the fan-run fiction site Archive of Our Own, popularly known as AO3. Now, a routine disruption has escalated into a crisis. What began as an estimated 12-hour unplanned outage has ballooned into a multi-week shutdown, leaving millions of users locked out of the site following a series of intermittent disruptions throughout the month.  An outage of this magnitude hit readers out of nowhere, landing with all the subtlety of a Looney Tunes anvil.

The platform is operated by the Organization for Transformative Works. An update posted Thursday to the site’s status page and shared via Bluesky and Tumblr said that service restoration will take at least two weeks, possibly four. 

“We are hopeful that we will be able to bring the site back up in a degraded state sooner,” the update said. “If that does happen, there may be times when the site has to be brought down temporarily until this is fully resolved.”

			

More from CNET

That update followed an initial notification, 12 hours earlier, with the announcement that “AO3 maintenance is in progress. We expect it to take at least 12 hours, but it may take longer.”

In response to a CNET request for more information, an OTW representative pointed to a new status update, saying, “The statement confirms that the downtime is a security incident, the scope of which is still being assessed. I can let you know that this is not related to the PHP security issue as the Archive uses Ruby on Rails.”

According to the update, “Earlier today, we detected evidence of a security incident on AO3. We are still in the early stages of response to this security incident and determining its scope. AO3 will remain down while we continue investigating and addressing what has been found so far.”

It emphasizes that no data has been deleted, and while they don’t think user data was compromised, they can’t rule it out and recommend you change your password if it’s not unique to AO3. (It should be if you practice safe password practices.) Donor information resides in a separate, unconnected database.

If you need a stopgap for your fanfic needs, you can try Wattpad or FanFiction.  The r/DeletedFanfiction Reddit, Bluesky members and other communities have stepped up to offer copies of works they’d already downloaded and to crowdsource alternatives.

title: Apple fined $15.5 million as South Korea orders changes to App Store rules
snippet: Apple and Google were fined today in South Korea over their app payment practices, with regulators also ordering both companies to change several policies. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Apple and Google were fined today in South Korea over their app payment practices, with regulators also ordering both companies to change several policies. Here are the details.

Apple’s App Store woes keep mounting

South Korea’s Korea Media and Communications Commission (KMCC) announced today a series of fines and corrective orders against Apple and Google over violations of the country’s Telecommunications Business Act.

Specifically for Apple, the KMCC imposed a fine of 20.81 billion won (approximately $15.5 million) and ordered the company to revise its App Store policies regarding payment methods and app review procedures, as well as prevent what it referred to as “discriminatory commission” practices from recurring.

In its announcement, the KMCC noted:

This is the first enforcement case under the 2021 amendment to the Telecommunications Business Act, which introduced prohibited acts for app market operators, such as forcing specific payment methods and unfairly delaying app reviews.

In essence, the decision centers around three violations: forcing specific payment methods, unfairly delaying app reviews, and imposing discriminatory commissions.

On the payment methods front, the KMCC said Apple and Google “effectively forced” developers to use their own in-app payment systems by imposing a 26% commission and additional restrictions on third-party alternatives.

“This constitutes an act in which an app market operator unfairly uses its position in transactions to force mobile content providers and others to use a specific payment method,” the KMCC said.

As a result, Apple and Google must revise their policies to allow external payment methods and address restrictions imposed on developers using alternative payment systems.

As for the app review process, the KMCC found that Apple and Google “delayed app reviews, for example by not providing specific reasons when reviews were delayed or not clearly responding to individual inquiries about the reasons for delays and expected timelines.”

Accordingly, Apple and Google must revise their app review procedures to address these issues.

Finally, on the discriminatory commissions, which applied only to Apple, the KMCC found that between July 2015 and January 2023, the company calculated its 30% commission differently for South Korean and overseas developers. While overseas developers were charged based on prices excluding value-added tax (VAT), South Korean developers were charged based on prices including VAT.

“KMCC determined that this constituted an act of unfairly providing rates, numbers, telecommunications facilities, or other economic benefits for telecommunications services or bundled services in a discriminatory manner compared to other users […].”

The KMCC said Apple will also have to take measures to prevent discriminatory commission practices between South Korean and overseas developers from recurring.

According to Reuters, Apple said it “‌disagreed ⁠with the decision and was evaluating options in accordance with South Korean ​laws.” ​Apple added that “⁠it has worked with outside developers ​to enable innovation ​through ⁠its App Store.”

Today’s decision comes on the heels of similar regulatory pressure in other markets, including Brazil and Japan, where Apple has introduced alternative app distribution and payment options in response to local competition rules.

The company has also faced years of scrutiny in the European Union, where it recently overhauled its App Store fees and business terms to address concerns raised by the European Commission.

title: MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR looks awesome, but I’m not rushing to upgrade
snippet: After five years, Apple released its first major MacBook Pro overhaul since the M1 Pro/M1 Max models, and well… it was a little bit underwhelming from a design perspective. The product is incredible on many merits, but after seeing it, I’m not left feeling like I need to buy one – at least not yet. more…
fullText:
After five years, Apple released its first major MacBook Pro overhaul since the M1 Pro/M1 Max models, and well… it was a little bit underwhelming from a design perspective. The product is incredible on many merits, but after seeing it, I’m not left feeling like I need to buy one – at least not yet.

‘Overhaul’ wasn’t much of one

The new MacBook Pro is substantially lighter. That’s a major improvement, especially if you’re someone who carries around a 16-inch MacBook Pro. With this new PROLED XDR generation, the 14-inch model reduced in weight by 0.5 pounds, and the 16-inch model reduced by 0.7 pounds. That’s a great deal when you’re carrying it around in a backpack or similar. The new models are also marginally thinner.

For me, though, I find myself a bit surprised by the fact that nothing about the top case design changed. The keyboard, trackpad, speaker, and port layouts all look about the same, and the chassis didn’t change shape besides getting a bit thinner. For every MacBook Pro overhaul in the past, the top case has changed in a meaningful way. With this overhaul, it really feels like more of a display upgrade that’s also accompanied by a lighter chassis.

Was there anything wrong with the current MacBook Pro chassis? Not at all. However, you could also argue the same for most design shifts in Apple’s history. It would’ve been nice to have a slightly different look, beyond the display.

Expensive, and the chips aren’t a major upgrade

This is more of a personal point. That said, I already have an M4 Pro model, and given the fact that these new MacBook Pros are substantially more expensive ($400 more compared to the miniLED MacBook Pros, which are also $300 more than they were prior to the June price hikes), I’m not particularly excited to buy silicon that isn’t the latest and greatest. The M5 family kicked off last year, and we already know M7 is coming next year.

I fully understand why Apple opted to skip the M6 Pro and M6 Max chips, but it sure does make this MacBook Pro feel ever so slightly more uninteresting.

Touch isn’t a huge selling point

Apple already alluded to the fact that they have more in the pipeline when it comes to macOS optimizations for touch, so maybe I’ll be wowed in the future. For now though, aside from being able to interact with the iOS simulator with proper touch, I don’t really see much of a need to have touch on my Mac. 

It’s great that it’s there, and I’m certainly not disappointed that Apple added it – but I’m not yet convinced I truly need it.

Wrap up

None of this was to bash on the new MacBook Pro at all. In fact, I’ll most definitely be buying one in the future, most likely once it gains M7 Pro and M7 Max chips by this time next year. Hopefully touch feels more important by then. I certainly love the idea of having a glowing Apple logo again, just not quite yet – and it’s not like this product will be going anywhere if I don’t buy it during the first iteration.

	

It’s also worth noting I haven’t yet seen the new display in person. It’s totally possible I’ll be blown away once I see it, but I still think I’ll be capable of waiting. Especially since my M4 Pro MacBook Pro already has a 1000 nit display, so I’m not missing out too terribly from the OLED model.

How do you feel about the new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR? Will you be buying one, or are you in a similar boat as I am? Let us know in the comments.

Good morning! Today I’m reading about the death of the internet, deciding whether to buy a PROLED or many pro LEDs, building all my IKEA furniture with this step-by-step 3D app, trying desperately to get into the Readwise Books early access, and playing an “Enhanced 3D” Command & Conquer: Red Alert on my PC.

Inbox is the tech newsletter that goes beyond the news cycle. We cover the most important 9to5Google stories from the last couple of days along with a few highlights from around the web. We publish every Tuesday and Thursday, and if you like what you read, please subscribe.

Inbox is written by Daniel Bader. Read previous issues here, and then catch up with Ben Schoon’s excellent Weekender column published every Sunday.

⭐️ Starred

Alphabet’s Q3 earnings were interesting. Despite a 25% rise in revenue and a healthy net income of $26 billion, analysts were disappointed with the company’s results, sending the stock down as much as 11% in after-hours trading.

	

On the plus side, the company’s cloud business is booming, doubling year-over-year revenue to $30 billion as it attracts frontier labs to its data centers. But advertising revenue didn’t meet expectations, and investors appear to be worried that its search advertising business, one of the most efficient sources of recurring revenue in history, is not keeping up with changing user behavior.

As Anthropic gets ready to soar into its IPO later this year, mature businesses like Alphabet, Microsoft, and Amazon are racing to adapt to a market where demand for AI infrastructure is outpacing compute supply. But investors are looking at the capital expenditure tied up in future data center buildouts and getting nervous that, if the bubble bursts, even these well-capitalized companies will take massive hits.

The biggest question surrounding Google’s stock performance is whether it can sufficiently monetize AI-powered search before demand for its traditional search inventory falls off a cliff. As the company sends less and less traffic to the open web, it’s touting the fact that AI Mode and AI Overviews keep people on Google for three times as long as traditional search.

So it’s no surprise that it’s expanding ads in AI Mode to 10 new markets this week, with more to come by the end of the year. While the post was only a few paragraphs long, expanding its AI ad business may end up being one of the company’s most consequential announcements of 2026.

✉️ Inbox

OnePlus rolling out ColorOS to OnePlus 13, others as Android 17 update expands. Mixed feelings about this one, but glad to see OPPO is honoring its promise to OnePlus owners.

Android Find Hub app reveals how ‘Left Behind’ and ‘Ring your phone’ alerts work on Pixel Tag. Hard to believe the Pixel Tag still isn’t available given it was announced in August.

Vivo’s X500 series launches globally with MediaTek chips and insane cameras. Like the OPPO Find X10 Max, Vivo’s new flagship is ridiculous in all the best ways.

Someone is bringing Android Auto back to your phone’s screen, and it actually works. This little sideloaded hack fakes Android Auto on your smartphone for those who don’t want to deal with Google’s current disaster of a solution.

Gemini Notebook for Android, iOS adds built-in audio recorder. The best tool for cheating on optimizing your homework just got even better.

Samsung’s open-ear Galaxy Buds On cost $229 in the US, launching next month. They’re no Beans, and they’re also very expensive. Good luck with these, Samsung.

Samsung can’t decide between a larger Galaxy Z Fold 9 or one with worse specs, and neither can I. Here’s my hot take: we need fewer, not more, foldable options. Keep the lineup focused.

Motorola’s flagship Signature 27 sounds quite expensive in retail leak. Motorola is cooking lately, but this phone looks a little too rich for my blood.

Public Discord messages might start showing up in Google Search, unless users opt out

RAMageddon is ready to rage on through 2030. We get the world we deserve, and that means more expensive gadgets on which to use many, many AI tokens.

Amazon’s latest Echo smart displays and speakers reinforce Google Home’s lost lead. I’m no fan of Alexa, but I have to admit Amazon is crushing it on the hardware design front lately.

Google adding more Connected Apps to Gemini & Search with new dev platform. Android’s Dev Summit yielded some really interesting announcements, and this was top among them.

Google Chrome rolling out ‘Suggested by Gemini’ autofill.

Google announces Gemini 4 Carbon with ‘significant gains across coding and agentic tasks’. Two weeks after Argon comes Carbon. What happened to Barium? Guess it was stuck in the loo.

Some Pixel Watch users report a sudden decrease in battery life

➡️ FWD:

I didn’t get to see either of the first Dune movies on IMAX, but you can bet your ass I’ve already secured opening-day tickets for the third one. Dune: Part Three debuts in December, and we now have the final trailer that showcases the impending showdown between Muad’Dib and Chani as the former realizes the consequences of his galactic war.

On the gadgety side, there’s another impending showdown brewing between XREAL’s Android XR-powered Aura glasses and Meta’s upcoming VR Glasses. 

I liked Jasmine Uniza’s video below comparing the two because, until I watched it, I didn’t realize the extent of the diverging approaches to reality they’re each taking. The Aura glasses are more traditionally translucent and somewhat awkwardly project two OLED screens on top of the dimmed lenses, allowing the outside world to filter through. Meta’s VR Glasses eschew the traditional headset shape and weight of the Quest but block out far more of the outside world and use external cameras, like their predecessors, to pipe in mixed-reality footage.

Finally, some personal news of a sort: I am now a permanent host of The Sideload. If you know me at all, you know I love a podcast, and Will Sattelberg was my co-host at the Android Police podcast for three years before he left for 9to5 last year. I’m so excited to be doing this again every week with him, and I hope you’ll tune in to our most recent episode about the death of the web browser and other good news.
